body.en: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, eight angles appear — but only two distinct measures. Knowing which pairs are equal and which are supplementary unlocks most angle-chase problems.
Corresponding angles are equal; alternate (interior or exterior) angles are equal; co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary, summing to \( 180^{\circ} \).

Corresponding angles (such as ∠1 and ∠5) occupy the same relative position at each intersection and are congruent.

body.en:
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One interior angle is \( 72^{\circ} \). Find its alternate interior angle.

Alternate interior angles are equal:

\[ 72^{\circ}. \]

A co-interior angle measures \( 110^{\circ} \). Find the other co-interior angle.

\[ 180^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=70^{\circ}. \]

label.en: Common Pitfall — Conflating Alternate and Consecutive Angles

body.en: A frequent error on SAT and ACT geometry questions is equating consecutive (same-side) interior angles instead of setting their sum to \( 180^{\circ} \). Remember the letter shapes: Z-angles (alternate interior) are equal; F-angles (corresponding) are equal; but C-angles (consecutive interior) are supplementary.

label.en: Worked Example C — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 4 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 9 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (4)^2 + (9)^2 = 16 + 81 = \mathbf{97} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(4)(9) = \mathbf{18} \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 5 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 5 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (5)^2 + (5)^2 = 25 + 25 = \mathbf{50} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = \mathbf{12.5} \).

question.en: Two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal line. Two consecutive interior angles have measures \( (3x - 10)^{\circ} \) and \( (2x + 25)^{\circ} \). Find the measure of the acute angle.

solution.en:
Solution: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary, so they sum to \( 180^{\circ} \):

\[ (3x - 10) + (2x + 25) = 180 \implies 5x + 15 = 180 \implies 5x = 165 \implies x = 33. \]

Substitute \( x = 33 \) into both angle expressions:

\[ 3(33) - 10 = 89^{\circ}, \quad 2(33) + 25 = 91^{\circ}. \]

The acute angle has measure \( 89^{\circ} \).

question.en: Two parallel lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are cut by a transversal \(T\). A pair of alternate exterior angles are given by \((7x - 14)^{\circ}\) and \((4x + 31)^{\circ}\). Find the value of \(x\) and the measure of each alternate exterior angle.

solution.en:
Step 1: Set up the equation using alternate exterior angles: Alternate exterior angles created by parallel lines are congruent:

\[ 7x - 14 = 4x + 31 \implies 3x = 45 \implies x = 15. \]

Step 2: Evaluate the angle measure:

\[ 7(15) - 14 = 105 - 14 = 91^{\circ}. \]

Check: \(4(15) + 31 = 60 + 31 = 91^{\circ}\). Both alternate exterior angles measure \(91^{\circ}\).

question.en: [Lines & Angles · Practice 3] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 5t + 5 \), evaluate \( g(8) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 50 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 8 \): \( g(8) = 5(8) + 5 = \mathbf{45} \). Setting \( 5t + 5 = 50 \) gives \( 5t = 45 \implies t = \mathbf{9} \).

question.en: [Lines & Angles · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
